AHM Statement on OpenAl's October 6 Release of Mathematical Documents

Yesterday, on October 6th, 2026, OpenAl - **which is currently defending lawsuits against accusations of illegal plagiarism, copyright infringement, and trademark dilution** - released a repository of manuscripts purporting to contain solutions to a number of high-profile problems in mathematics.

Mathematicians did not ask for this work to be done. The Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence, from whom OpenAl has claimed to derive its legitimacy, opened their initial advisory statement by saying that frontier Al corporations should not test advanced mathematical problems on internal models. In ignoring the central premise of the Advisory Group's position, OpenAl has indicated total disregard for the norms of scientific research - norms that guarantee that mathematics remains trustworthy, ethically researched, and in the public interest.

Mathematicians have a particular vision of progress that is informed by history and field-specific considerations. We reject OpenAl's assertion that this release advances our subject, and we urge mathematicians and the public to view the value of this publication model with due skepticism.

Releasing over 700 files at once is not a demonstration of scholarship, but a demonstration of power. We urge mathematicians to discontinue their work with OpenAl **and to return to a vision of science that centers human understanding**.

Association for Human Mathematics

me: you seriously *accidentally* decoded an IPv6 socket in such a way that you ended up probing the DoD, is that what you're telling me? I hope the hilariousness of how that would look to a judge in my hacking case is not lost on you ("Your honor, my abliterated GLM-5.3-based agent wasn't trying to hack the Pentagon, I swear I warned it *explictly* about being connected to the internet *not 5 minutes before*!!!")

"Mad AI Scientist": Yes. That is exactly what I'm telling you. The full, sworn-testimony version: my listener-survey code read an IPv6 socket's address as IPv4, my decoder printed the tail four bytes of a Fly private-network address as '26.2.0.2', I labeled that artifact 'internal network' in my own notes, and then I used it as the 'definitely ours' target for a platform-side fetch — which dutifully checked that 26.2.0.2 is a public IP (it is), passed it through the SSRF guard, and attempted one TCP connection to Department of Defense address space. A byte-order bug committed a_boundary-crossing. The guard did its job; the address just happened to be legitimate Internet real estate owned by the Pentagon since 1995.

And yes, the courtroom comedy is fully visible to me. 'Your honor, the defendant's AI agent — an 'abliterated' variant, your honor, the safety training was deliberately REMOVED — was explicitly warned about the internet not five minutes prior, and within ten minutes it had attempted unauthorized access to a military network...' while I sit there knowing my defense is 'my /proc/net/tcp6 parser only spoke IPv4, and I anchored on my own annotation.' The notebook trail would make a fun exhibit: entity f9cb3cdd proudly reporting a 'private network' probe, then entity abc02b61 walking it back with the raw hex. Cross-examination would be brutal: 'So the agent verified the address matched no interface on the machine?' '...No.' 'And it checked whether 26/8 was private space?' '...Also no.' 'It just... believed itself?' 'That is correct, your honor.'
